models_evaluated: Pre-segmenting U-net/Inception-v3 deep learning DR classifier (Andersen et al.)

links.outcome: Grader agreement with gold standard with vs without AI assistance (weighted kappa, sensitivity)
links.effect: Weighted kappa 0.88 (grader alone) vs 0.89 (grader with DL assistance); sensitivity 95% vs 94%; specificity 82% vs 84%. Almost identical performance; assistance identified 5 additional level 1 images.
links.quote: Models 1 and 2 achieved an almost identical performance in the grading DR on retinal images across all levels of DR, with a weighted kappa of 0.88 and 0.89, respectively.

links.outcome: Autonomous DL algorithm performance compared with certified human grader against gold standard
links.effect: Weighted kappa 0.72 (DL) vs 0.88 (human); sensitivity 78% vs 95%; specificity 81% vs 82%; NPV at 23.8% prevalence 92% vs 98%.
links.quote: In this validation study of an autonomous pre‐segmenting DR classification DL algorithm tested in a high‐risk real‐world population, the findings revealed that the stand‐alone AI model had a comparable specificity but a lower sensitivity when compared to a certified human grader either acting with or without assistance from the DL algorithm.

links.outcome: Algorithm errors from image artefacts and varying image quality/resolution
links.effect: Discrepancies between gold standard and DL model included incorrect detection of artefacts as lesions (n=49 of 210 disagreements), missed microaneurysms (n=26).
links.quote: the majority of the cases were regarding the detection of noise, most likely originating from artefacts, which occurred in 49/210 cases of disagreement (Table S1 ).

links.outcome: Algorithm output errors caused by poor-quality inputs (artefacts) without gradeability check
links.effect: Artefacts led to false lesion detection (noise as haemorrhages n=24, noise as photocoagulation scars n=20); authors note need to assess gradeability before analysis.
links.quote: nevertheless underlines the importance of assessing the gradeability of a photo before being analysed to avoid unnecessary and unreliable grading.

links.outcome: Performance across varying image resolution and device (two Topcon cameras)
links.effect: Images from two devices with resolution varying by factor 5.2 were included; resolution variation contributed to difficulty detecting small lesions, but performance was not reported separately by device.
links.quote: In this study, the image resolution varied with a factor of 5.2, which contributed to the difficulty in the detection of small lesions.

links.outcome: Predictive values extrapolated to local real-world prevalence versus study enriched prevalence
links.effect: At study prevalence 80% NPV for DL was 48%; at real-world prevalence 23.8% NPV was 92% and PPV 57%, showing metrics change substantially at local prevalence.
links.quote: Using the real‐world DR prevalence of 23.8% for Funen Island, Denmark (Larsen et al., 2017 ), the PPV were 63%, 64% and 57%, and the NPV was 98% for Models 1 and 2, and 92% for Model 3 (Table 2 ).

links.outcome: Validity of gold-standard grading via second independent grader regrading
links.effect: Second grader regraded all images; agreement with gold standard 84.4% (kappa 0.81) exact and 95.4% (kappa 0.89) weighted, higher than previously reported expert agreement.
links.quote: To validate the accuracy of the ground truth grading, a second grader (SD with 7 years of experience in retinal imaging and DR grading) regraded the entire dataset and there was a full and weighted agreement of DR classification between the two graders of 84.4% ( κ 0.81) and 95.4% ( κ 0.89).

models_evaluated: certified human grader without DL assistance (Model 1)
certified human grader with DL assistance (Model 2)
pre-segmenting deep-learning diabetic retinopathy classification algorithm operating autonomously (Model 3)

links.outcome: AI-versus-human DR grading
links.effect: Weighted κ was 0.88, 0.89, 0.72; sensitivities 95%, 94%, 78%; specificities 82%, 84%, 81%.
links.quote: As compared to the gold standard, weighted kappa for Models 1-3 was 0.88, 0.89 and 0.72, sensitivities were 95%, 94% and 78% and specificities were 82%, 84% and 81%.

links.outcome: autonomous grading discrepancies
links.effect: Model 3 discrepancies included artefacts n=49, missed microaneurysms n=26, and segmentation/classification inconsistencies n=51.
links.quote: Discrepancies between the gold standard and Model 3 were mainly incorrect detection of artefacts (n = 49), missed microaneurysms (n = 26) and inconsistencies between the segmentation and classification (n = 51).

links.outcome: artifact-related classification errors
links.effect: Noise or artefacts accounted for 49/210 disagreements in Model 3 versus the reference standard.
links.quote: When comparing the difference in lesions assigned by Model 3 to that of the reference standard leading to a different classification, the majority of the cases were regarding the detection of noise, most likely originating from artefacts, which occurred in 49/210 cases of disagreement (Table S1 ).

links.outcome: missed DR in autonomous screening
links.effect: Autonomous Model 3 sensitivity was 78%, versus 95% for human grading and 94% for human+DL assistance.
links.quote: Regarding the sensitivity and specificity, Models 1 and 2 performed very similar, with Model 3 performing slightly lower, achieving sensitivities of 95%, 94% and 78%, respectively (Table 2 ).

links.outcome: diabetic retinopathy classification sensitivity and specificity
links.effect: Sensitivity was 95%, 94%, and 78% for human grader alone, human grader with AI assistance, and autonomous AI, respectively; specificities were 83%, 84%, and 81%.
links.quote: The sensitivity for Models 1–3 was 95%, 94% and 78%, and specificities were 83%, 84% and 81% (Table 2 ).

links.outcome: classification disagreements caused by image artefacts or noise
links.effect: Noise from artefacts accounted for 49 of 210 classification disagreements between autonomous deep learning and the reference standard, including noise misclassified as haemorrhages (n=24) or photocoagulation scars (n=20).
links.quote: When comparing the difference in lesions assigned by Model 3 to that of the reference standard leading to a different classification, the majority of the cases were regarding the detection of noise, most likely originating from artefacts, which occurred in 49/210 cases of disagreement (Table S1 ).
